newsitem.title: INDIA: Philippines' Ramos quiet on India's APEC, UN bids.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' Ramos quiet on India's APEC, UN bids.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos on Tuesday urged South and East Asia to tighten links but stopped short of supporting India's efforts to join the APEC forum or become a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council.

On the third day of a four-day visit to the Indian capital, Ramos said it was becoming difficult to distinguish between the economies of East and South Asia now that most countries were opening up to trade and investment.

"It is in that light that I now propose that East Asia on the one hand and India and other countries of South Asia on the other begin to explore, intensively, measures to link their markets and economies much more closely," he said.

The Philippine president told a group of business leaders that the neighbouring regions could bring down cross-border trade barriers, expand air and shipping links and step up economic and technical cooperation. He proposed that ministers of planning, finance and agriculture consult regularly.

But in an interview with Reuters, Ramos would not explicitly endorse India's campaign to join either the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum or the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The 18 APEC members from Asia, North America and South America have put on hold any new members, and may consider expansion at a meeting in Canada set for mid-1997, Ramos said.
"However I will not answer your question now because everything we do in APEC is also by consensus, just like in ASEAN," he told Reuters.

Ramos said India was a full dialogue partner in the seven-nation ASEAN. Asked if he supported India's drive to become a full member, he said the regional grouping was considering taking in Cambodia, Laos and Burma. "It (ASEAN) is confined to Southeast Asia," he said.

Ramos, whose six-year term of elected office ends next year, said developing countries with global political and economic influence should be represented on the U.S. Security Council as permanent members.
The council currently has five permanent members -- Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States -- and 10 others which rotate as non-members.

Asked if he was prepared specifically to support India's campaign to become a permanent member, Ramos said: "We express our support for the big countries that are now acquiring or have acquired major economic and political influence."
On Monday, Ramos, who said his country was seeking military equipment and technology from India, discussed regional security issues with Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.

The Philippine leader said he did not consider India to be a "counter-weight" to China in the region. China, along with the four other permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, is a declared nuclear power. India exploded a nuclear device in 1974 and is believed to be capable of building the bomb.

"We are asking India to continue to play that important role of advocacy of independence and moderation, fair play and non-violence, and should not confine itself to just South Asia which is the conventional wisdom right now," he said.
Ramos said most countries had signed the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty to ban nuclear weapons tests, but India had chosen not to do so. "That's India's solution," he said. "I cannot speak for India."
Ramos was scheduled to leave for Dhaka on Wednesday.
